health-tech-ddc23f4601.headline: Sun Pharma's US deal signals new template for Indian drugmakers
health-tech-ddc23f4601.fulltext:
Sun Pharma's US deal signals new template for Indian drugmakers
Sun Pharma has struck a deal with the US government to lower medicine prices and expand manufacturing in America. The agreement signals a possible shift for Indian drugmakers towards strategic bargaining and localised production in the US.
When Sun Pharma struck a deal with the US government to lower prices for certain medicines and expand its American manufacturing commitments, it did more than secure relief from a potentially punishing tariff regime. It may have offered Indian drugmakers a glimpse of what doing business in the world’s largest pharmaceutical market could increasingly look like.
The bargain is significant: access and protection in exchange for lower prices, greater transparency and a deeper manufacturing footprint in the US.
For Indian pharmaceutical companies, which have built a formidable business by manufacturing medicines efficiently in India and exporting them across the world, that could mark a structural shift.
The question is no longer simply whether Indian companies can sell more medicines in the US: it is whether they may increasingly have to make more of them there too.
Namit Joshi, chairman of the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil), sees the Sun Pharma-US government agreement as potentially beneficial for both sides.
“I see the Sun-US govt deal as a win-win for both,” he says, adding that more companies could explore a similar route. Such agreements, he argues, can reduce uncertainty and ease pressure on companies' profitability.
But there is an equally important caveat: India cannot allow its pharmaceutical export strategy to become excessively dependent on one market. Indian companies, Joshi says, also need to continue expanding elsewhere.
That balancing act may define the next phase of India's pharmaceutical export story.
A DEAL WITH CONSEQUENCES
Sun Pharma is among nine additional pharmaceutical companies that signed agreements with the Trump administration under its Most-Favoured-Nation, or MFN, drug-pricing push.
The White House says these deals are aimed at bringing US drug prices closer to the lowest prices paid in other developed countries, while also encouraging companies to invest in American manufacturing and strengthen domestic drug supply chains.
For Sun Pharma, the agreement provides tariff relief in exchange for commitments linked to drug pricing and the broader US pharmaceutical supply chain. Under the administration's policy, companies that enter MFN pricing agreements and meet approved onshoring commitments can receive preferential tariff treatment, including a temporary zero-tariff rate under specified conditions.
The logic behind the deal is therefore straightforward but consequential: the US government offers regulatory and tariff certainty, while pharmaceutical companies agree to help lower medicine prices and increase their strategic presence inside the US.
That could become an increasingly attractive proposition for Indian companies with large American businesses.
“I see the Sun Pharma deal as a template, but I don’t think it will be replicated uniformly,” pharma analyst Salil Kallianpur told India Today.
The companies most likely to consider such a model, he says, would be those “for whom the US is strategically indispensable and where higher-value portfolios can absorb the cost of localisation.”
This point is important because for a company selling large volumes of low-margin generic medicines, building and maintaining expensive US manufacturing infrastructure may make little financial sense.
But companies with speciality medicines, complex generics, injectables and differentiated products may be better placed to trade higher costs for greater pricing power, regulatory certainty and political goodwill.
According to Shrikant Akolkar, veteran pharma analyst with Nuvama Institutional Equities, only Sun among Indian companies seem to be fitting the bill for how the US administration wants to operate with pharma companies from abroad currently, but Kallianpur identifies Dr Reddy's, Aurobindo, Lupin and Zydus as companies worth watching, although the rationale differs for each.
HOW MEDICINE SYSTEM WORKS IN THE US
To understand why such a deal matters, it is important to understand an unusual feature of the US healthcare market: the manufacturer is only one part of the drug-pricing chain.
Healthcare in the US is largely insurance-driven. Unlike India, where health insurance has traditionally focused largely on hospitalisation, American insurance coverage also extends to prescription medicines for a substantial share of the population.
The drug, however, moves through a complex commercial ecosystem.
Large distributors procure medicines from manufacturers and supply them through the healthcare and pharmacy network. Pharmacy Benefit Managers, or PBMs, negotiate prices and rebates between drug manufacturers, insurers and pharmacies. Companies such as CVS Health's pharmacy benefit business, Cigna and OptumRx are among the major players in this ecosystem.
The stated objective is to use purchasing power to obtain lower prices. But critics argue that the system has become opaque and that the financial incentives of intermediaries can distort what patients ultimately pay.
This system, says the Trump administration repeatedly, should be disrupted.
And the MFN pricing push is a step in that direction – seeking to address one of the biggest political paradoxes in American healthcare: medicines that are often sold more cheaply in other wealthy countries can cost significantly more in the US.
At the same time, the administration is pursuing another objective – reducing the US' dependence on overseas pharmaceutical manufacturing. The April 2026 proclamation on pharmaceutical imports explicitly links drug affordability with supply-chain security and the expansion of domestic manufacturing.
In other words, Washington's emerging formula appears to be: lower prices for Americans, more manufacturing in America and less strategic dependence on foreign supply chains.
INDIA'S MANUFACTURING DILEMMA
For India, however, localisation in America presents both an opportunity and a risk.
Indian drugmakers have become globally competitive precisely because of India's manufacturing ecosystem – its skilled workforce, scale, established plants and relatively lower production costs. If companies increasingly need to maintain manufacturing ecosystems on both sides of the world, those cost advantages could begin to erode.
Kallianpur warns of exactly this possibility. “The important distinction, however, is where the investment occurs,” he says.
If Indian companies merely expand formulation manufacturing in the US while continuing to import active pharmaceutical ingredients, intermediates and key starting materials from elsewhere, “that would not be building supply-chain resilience.”
The deeper challenge for India, therefore, is not simply to prevent factories from moving abroad. It is to move further up the pharmaceutical value chain.
Kallianpur argues that the real prize lies in expanding India's capabilities in active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), intermediates, complex chemistry, biologics, contract development and manufacturing services, and advanced manufacturing.
That is particularly important because a geographically diversified supply chain is not necessarily a resilient one. A tablet may be manufactured in the US, but if its critical ingredients originate from a highly concentrated overseas supply base, strategic dependence has merely changed its location.
The Sun Pharma deal, therefore, raises a bigger question for India: should it view US localisation as the loss of Indian manufacturing – or as an opportunity to retain higher-value stages of the pharmaceutical supply chain at home while companies expand globally?
US STILL MATTERS
Despite the recent decline in exports, the US remains far too important for Indian drugmakers to ignore.
India's pharmaceutical exports to the US stood at $9.47 billion in FY26, down nearly 10% from the previous year, according to Pharmexcil data. The decline reflected a combination of a high base, generic price erosion, inventory correction and product-cycle factors rather than a fundamental collapse in demand.
Indeed, Namit Joshi has described the slowdown as “not a structural concern”, pointing to the continued strength of the US market and opportunities in specialty generics and injectables.
The longer-term trend also tells a more reassuring story.
India's overall pharmaceutical exports reached about $30.5 billion in FY25, up 9.4% from the previous year and representing a dramatic expansion from just $1.9 billion in 2000-01.
The US has been central to that growth even though the story is now shifting rapidly, even though Indian companies have played a substantial role in keeping American medicines affordable.
Industry estimates cited in an IQVIA assessment have found that Indian-made medicines generated hundreds of billions of dollars in savings for the US healthcare system over the past decade, while Indian companies have become particularly important suppliers across several high-volume generic therapy areas.
That dependence creates leverage for Indian manufacturers – but it also creates exposure.
The Sun Pharma agreement could encourage other Indian drugmakers to negotiate their own arrangements with Washington. But Kallianpur's warning is worth remembering: a template is not the same as a blueprint.
Not every company can afford US localisation. Not every portfolio has the margins to absorb it. And not every manufacturer has the same strategic dependence on the US.
“The companies that can make that additional cost economically productive through higher-value products, better pricing power and greater regulatory and political credibility will come out stronger,” Kallianpur says.
That could accelerate a wider transformation already underway in Indian pharma – from commoditised, price-sensitive generics towards speciality medicines, complex formulations, biologics and other differentiated products.
For India, the most important outcome may ultimately depend on what happens at home.
If US manufacturing commitments simply pull higher-value pharmaceutical capacity out of India, the country's traditional cost advantage could gradually weaken. But if Indian companies use their growing global footprints to build more sophisticated research, API, biologics and advanced manufacturing ecosystems within India, the shift could strengthen the industry.
Sun Pharma's deal, then, is bigger than one company's tariff relief.
It may be an early signal that the next phase of the India-US pharmaceutical relationship will be shaped less by simple exports and more by strategic bargaining, local manufacturing and supply-chain security.

health-tech-2fb8ce1493.headline: FDA halts imports of Shoolin Pharma products to the US after inspection in India

FDA halts imports of Shoolin Pharma products to the US after inspection in India
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has halted imports into the United States of all products from Indian company Shoolin Pharma after finding unsanitary conditions at its facility in Gujarat state. The company produces active pharmaceutical ingredients for more than a dozen drugs, including medicines for erectile dysfunction and anticonvulsants.
Inspection observations
An FDA inspector visited the Shoolin Pharma facility in April. According to STAT News, the agency documented residue and stains on walls, floors, and production equipment, as well as corrosion on one of the production lines. One employee was wearing open-toed footwear.
The FDA also raised concerns about possible contamination in production and packaging areas. Separately, the regulator noted incomplete records of laboratory testing.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Supply restrictions
In August, the FDA halted all shipments of Shoolin Pharma products to the United States. The agency reported this in a warning letter dated August 18, which was later published on the FDA website. The letter also included photographs of conditions the regulator described as unsanitary.
Shoolin Pharma's active pharmaceutical ingredients were sold to US pharmacies that prepare medicines to order.

agritech-054ad357f8.headline: Sickles, sarees and smoke: Women on the frontlines of Uttarakhand forest fires
agritech-054ad357f8.fulltext:
- Uttarakhand is the most fire-prone state in the Indian Western Himalayas, where wildfire seasons are expanding — and women are taking the lead on fighting fires in their communities.
- Traditional gender roles assigning household and caregiving work to women is a reason why women are first responders to fire.
- In addition, many men have left rural villages in Uttarakhand to search for opportunities elsewhere; women often stay behind for agriculture and feel obliged to protect their land and animals.
- Despite a lack of formal employment, equipment and support for their firefighting work, Uttarakhand women successfully work to stop fires at their source, protecting their villages from hazard.
In the village forests of Uttarakhand, in the Himalayan region of northern India, a tree can be charred at its base while maintaining a green canopy at its peak. The distinct separation between burnt and unburnt wood is a physical marker of how high the flames reached. For the local women who rely on these woods for survival, the aftermath of wildfire means their daily chores take twice as long, forcing them deeper into the forest just to gather basic fodder and firewood when those closer to home are unusable.
Uttarakhand is the most fire-prone state in the Indian Western Himalayas, with increased fire incidence in the region coinciding with high-altitude warming that exceeds the global rate. Beyond individual fire events, the fire season itself is expanding. While the season usually lasts for about 12 weeks starting in mid-March, Uttarakhand now experiences winter fires, an alarming shift from what was previously snow season, hinting at a deeper ecosystem-level impact. This trend has only escalated, with the state recording a sharp spike in forest fire activity during the first four months of 2026.
This period is not just witnessed but experienced through each of the human senses. Trails of grey smoke engulf the bright blue sky. Along with the fog-like situation, the air carries soot, sometimes covering the roofs of houses with snow-like ash.
“We are all coughing our lungs out; during that time, our eyes are bloodshot, irritated by all the smoke, and it’s hard to breathe in the thick air. Even after days of fire, the firewood smell lingers,” said Tulsi Devi of Ayarpani village in Almora district.
While everyone endures the season, women predominate at the frontlines, fighting fires in Uttarakhand.
First responders born out of convention
Kavya Pandey, a researcher at the Centre for Wildlife Studies in Bangalore who has worked extensively on the relationship between women in Uttarakhand and forest fires, notes that traditional gender roles assigning household and caregiving work to women are why women are usually the first responders to wildfire. Since women’s daily labor keeps them in the forest for hours collecting firewood and fodder, they become, by default, the first line of defense.
Fighting fires can differ for both genders. To combat fires, the state forest department hires seasonal fire watchers, who are mostly men. Authorities also call women to help, but unlike men, they are rarely paid. Other than that, if fires occur at night, men often accompany women because of the danger from wild animals; but even in a group, the number of women is typically higher than that of men.
“If a woman sees fire anywhere, and she does not have a phone, she calls out to others by ululating or whistling, and all the women go together to snuff the fire,” said Kamla Devi, head of the Marhmanley village van panchayat, a community-managed village forest council that is unique to Uttarakhand.
Large-scale male migration compounds women’s role as firefighters. As climate change impacts agriculture with erratic rainfall, cloudbursts and drying water sources, men out-migrate in search of better opportunities. Research reveals that hundreds of villages in Uttarakhand are now depopulated, with many considered “ghost villages,” while hundreds more have lost half their population – mostly men, while women often stay behind for farming. Marhmanley reflects this pattern: Most of its men have left for the cities, leaving behind women, elders and children.
“With many migrating, fewer people are left to protect the village. The women who remain often have young children to look after, so they cannot leave,” Kamla said.
Deeply ingrained gender expectations also enforce these firefighting duties. Pandey argues that narratives framing women as natural protectors driven by “maternal instinct” have conditioned them to feel solely responsible.
“Even if there is a man when a fire breaks out, the man would scream, ‘Oh Basanti ki Ijja [Hey Basanti’s mother], there’s a fire,’ but what else would they do? How else will they tend their cattle?” said Kavya, explaining that it still remains a woman’s role to deal with fire.
This has always been the case, but firefighting is growing more difficult and more dangerous as fires expand with a shifting climate.
Higher stakes for women
Forest fires disrupt nearly every aspect of women’s lives. Around 71% of the total geographical area of Uttarakhand is forest area, supplying basic needs like drinking water, firewood and fodder for cattle grazing. With men working in cities, cattle rearing is one of the few ways rural women generate income.
“Forests are our everything. With active fires, we cannot even take our animals to graze. They stay tied in their sheds for days,” said Asha Devi of Bhetuli village.
Beyond daily chores, fires threaten homes and property. Most villages sit in close proximity to the forest. Marhmanley is one example, where houses are scattered along the hill’s incline. This positioning makes vigilance essential.
“We always keep a lookout for fires. We are afraid that if rocks roll down from the hill or if trees burn and fall downwards to the village, we have to protect trees and plants even if they are a distance away,” Kamla said.
Destruction and physical expense
Irrespective of age, when the forests burn, women run to extinguish them. Lila Devi, 70, still picks up her sickle to join the effort. “Amma [Granny] might look old, but she still runs like a goat on a hil,” Kamla laughed.
Women head out in groups, spacing themselves along the fire’s path in a chain to curb the flames faster and prevent embers or falling pine cones from spreading the blaze. Their main tool is a simple household sickle. Asha explained that they use sickles to cut green branches to make makeshift firebrooms (jhapa) to smother ground fires.
“When the flames are not too high, we use jhapa to beat back the fire. If they are [high], we clear a fireline instead; some of us push the fire back toward the already-burnt ground, while others use their sickle to pull away dry grass and twigs so it has nothing left to catch on,” Asha said.
A team of 10 can take an hour to tamp out a small fire, while a large fire means fighting flames all day. Long hours with limited tools and no protection leave many injured. Burnt hands, singed eyebrows and eyelashes are common.
“We fall and hit ourselves against rocks, but we don’t care for our well-being in that minute — all we care about is the forest. If it burns, what will our cattle eat?” Kamla said.
Safety guidelines recommend protective equipment, but local women rarely have access to it, and highly flammable synthetic nylon sarees remain common. Although Kamla advises wearing cotton clothes and proper shoes, the urgency leaves no time to change.
“We just run to the forest as we are. One year, my feet got severely burnt because we sometimes even found ourselves running with no slippers on. At the end of a shift, many of us are pricked by thorns,” Kamla said.
The danger escalates at night. Women lose sleep to keep watch over their homes and property, especially since many store stacks of dry hay near their houses. Asha, who lives half a kilometer from forests, has to guard the jungle at night.
“We’re scared for ourselves and our belongings. Last year, in November, a fire broke out at night. My son fell asleep, so I had to put it out alone. Two of my grass stacks burnt down,” Asha said.
Lifelong battles
Meena Bhoj sits on her bed, hands clasped tightly in her lap, her mind elsewhere. Her youngest of the three keeps popping up at the window beside her, calling out ‘mummy’ then ducking away again, giggling, waiting for her to look. Each time she does, Meena smiles back with her lips closed, careful not to show the tooth she chipped two years ago, on a firefighting run.
In June 2024, Meena spotted a fire across her home at 10 p.m. To save harvested pine needles meant for animal bedding, she and three other women, along with her brother-in-law, headed up the dark hill. After hours of work, the fire was put out. With only one flashlight between them, Meena navigated the steep descent alone.
“I was running down because there are leopards in the forest. I wanted to reach safety as quickly as I could. But I tripped,” Meena recalled.
She fell face-forward into a ditch, hitting her chest, cutting it and chipping her tooth.
“I was bleeding and in pain, but all I could do was go home and sleep it off,” Meena said.
She woke up with a swollen face and could not eat for days. Later, she had to undergo minor surgery on her chest. However, this was the least of her concerns.
Meena’s husband, Bhuvan Bhoj, was working as a fire watcher with the forest department. The day after Meena’s injury, Bhuvan was among the few who survived the Binsar fire tragedy, where six people died. Bhuvan still works with the forest department as a driver. “I am now disabled because of my injury; with these injuries, I cannot take up any job either,” Bhuvan said.
Meena is still haunted by bad dreams. Anytime she talks about the incident, her heart starts pounding. Despite the trauma, the couple still works against forest fires.
“I am scared of fire, but I am not scared for me; I am scared for him. I am constantly anxious when he goes to work. I call him multiple times a day to remind him not to get close to the fire,” Meena said as she looked down at her hands, trying to calm herself.
Policy disconnect
The trauma and lack of support have shifted perspectives for some.
“Now we just [extinguish] fires near our house, and we let the forest burn. Why should we risk our lives? Look what happened to Bhuvan and his family; did they get any compensation?” Chameli Devi, a 60-year-old living a few houses away from Meena, said angrily.
Bhuvan has yet to receive the 10 lakh rupees ($10,500) in compensation announced by Uttarakhand’s chief minister, a delay that has shaken villagers’ trust.
Binsar forest ranger Manoj Sanwal acknowledged the fire crisis, but stressed that the department is overburdened and underfunded. Though national policies allow support from police and disaster response forces, in practice, liability falls on forest staff, leaving unpaid local women to shoulder the burden.
Ironically, in regions where women perform the bulk of physical labor of firefighting, in practice, few are formally employed — unlike men. Seasonal fire watchers hired by the department are typically men; as reasons, officials cite safety and terrain, commenting that sarees make fieldwork risky. Despite being on the frontlines, women remain largely invisible in policy, rarely compensated, equipped or included in decision-making bodies.
Under the Forest Fire Prevention & Management Scheme, India introduced the National Action Plan on Forest Fire that incorporated a satellite-based system for timely detection and monitoring of forest fires. During peak fire seasons, operations rely on interdepartmental support from police and fire departments to national disaster response forces. They also lean on local communities, for hiring seasonal fire watchers. agritech-3c6b1a82be.headline: Mint Explainer: How a weak monsoon is fuelling India’s power surge and coal deficits
agritech-3c6b1a82be.fulltext:
India’s power demand surged to 256 gigawatts (GW) in the first week of September, leaving shortages above 20 million units. Driven by this growing demand, about 58 coal plants are now operating on critically low coal stocks, prompting miners to boost coal production and railway rake availability.
This combination of rising demand and supply deficits stems from a weaker monsoon, which has increased the use of irrigation pumps and household air conditioners.
Mint examines this surge in electricity demand and the reasons behind the coal and power shortfalls.
Why has power demand shot up of late?
A weaker monsoon has forced farmers to rely on groundwater pumping for irrigation, driving up power demand. Deficient rainfall has also created hot and humid conditions, leading to a surge in air conditioner usage. The demand for groundwater pumping is particularly high for paddy crops, which require substantial amounts of water during critical stages of growth.
After easing through July and August, electricity demand has begun climbing again, following a record peak demand of 270.8GW reached in May. During the first week of September, demand mostly remained above 255 GW. The Central Electricity Authority projects peak demand to touch 272 GW this year.
What’s driving the widening power deficit?
Along with the surge in demand, a drop in hydro power generation due to weaker monsoons has deepened the overall supply shortfall this year. Amid rainfall deficits, hydro generation fell 14% year-on-year in July, according to Crisil. A lag in coal production and supply logistics caused by rains, coupled with elevated power demand, further exacerbated this supply-demand mismatch.
Electricity shortages stayed above 20 million units during the first week of September—led by northern and western states—sharply higher than the less than 1 MU shortage recorded during the same period last year, when a healthy monsoon kept deficits minimal.
What is the coal stock situation at thermal power plants?
Coal inventories at thermal power plants have fallen in recent months. While stock depletion is typical during the monsoon, as rains disrupt mining while power demand climbs, the drawdown this year is far more acute due to the sudden demand surge. As of 6 September, total coal stock across the country's 190 thermal plants stood at 26.7 million tonnes—enough for an average of 8.5 days of operations. Of these, 58 plants are running on critical coal levels, holding less than 25% of their required inventory.
What measures are being taken to rebuild coal inventories?
Coal miners are stepping up shipments to thermal power plants, with state-run producers loading 444 railway rakes for the power sector on 6 September, up from 370 rakes on 3 September. Additionally, Coal India has seen output pick up as rains subside across its mining regions.
Average daily production by state-owned miners rose about 35% to 1.83 million tonnes on 6 September, compared to around 1.36 million tonnes over the first three days of the month. Coal India noted on 4 September that its mines were gearing up to resume full operational pace as rainfall eased, and would ensure higher output and movement as ground conditions improved.
Coal minister G Kishan Reddy said the country has more than 123 million tonnes of coal in mines, transit and thermal plants, which should be enough to meet 51 days of power demand. He added that supplies will increase as the rains subside.
Is India facing a power crisis?
The current supply tight spot cannot be classified as an outright crisis, as peak demand across the country is largely being met and coal dispatches have already increased. Elevated demand, driven significantly by groundwater pumping for paddy crops, is expected to persist through the end of this month. Furthermore, daytime electricity demand is largely met through solar power. Supply deficits primarily emerge during evening peak hours when solar output drops and thermal (coal-based) plants must step in.
India has so far been able to meet the high demand, despite instances of shortages. Even during the peak demand stretch in April-May, electricity needs were met through a diversified energy mix, including support from 20GW of gas-based power plants. Consequently, a major grid crisis is not expected going forward, though instances of load shedding may continue during this high-demand period.

indian-startups-5291c147be.headline: GalaxEye Secures US Patent for Satellite Imaging Tech
indian-startups-5291c147be.fulltext: In a first for an Indian spacetech startup, GalaxEye has got a US patent for satellite imaging technology, securing its landmark intellectual property that had already been patented in India. The patent covers the core architecture behind the startup’s proprietary OptoSAR technology, which synchronises optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sensors to collect spatially and temporally aligned earth observation data simultaneously from a single satellite over day and night. “This patented technology enables us to serve the global markets and provide weather agnostic imaging capabilities across sectors like defence, agriculture, insurance, disaster response and more,” said GalaxEye founder and CEO Suyash Singh. The grant of the patent comes on the heels of GalaxEye’s successful launch of its OptoSAR satellite Mission Drishti, its first satellite, back in May. Drishti, weighing around 190 kg, is India’s largest privately built earth observation satellite and the world’s first imaging satellite using OptoSAR. However, GalaxEye said it lost communication with Drishti in July after an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. It attributed the setback’s root cause to radiation effects from the event that likely impacted a critical onboard system. During its active operating phase over a few weeks, GalaxEye said that Mission Drishti successfully validated critical technologies, operational processes, and infrastructure required to design, build, launch, and operate advanced space systems. The startup is now targeting the launch of two new OptoSAR satellites within the next two years while expanding its in-house capabilities to further strengthen quality, reliability, and execution. Founded in 2021 by Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye is building multi-sensor earth observation satellites. Last month, it acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps to deepen its in-house satellite engineering capabilities. It is planning further launches with a target of scaling towards a 30-satellite constellation over the next five years. It claims to have a growing pipeline of domestic and international customers across sectors. The IIT Madras-incubated startup has raised $26.9 Mn in funding to date from investors like Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, Rainmatter, and Anicut Capital. Most recently, it raised a ₹44 Cr tranche in March as part of its ongoing Series A round, Inc42 learnt. Zooming out, the involvement of private players in the space ecosystem has been deepening over the past few years. Investors, too, are queuing up to back spacetech startups. According to Inc42 data, the funding in the sector surged 94% to $157 Mn in 2025 from $81 Mn in 2024, with the broader market set to cross $77 Bn by 2030.

The company unveiled the Stage Testing & Inspection Facility (STIF) and the Pressurant Tank Realisation, Over-wrapping and Outfitting Facility (PROOF) at its assembly and testing facility. The facilities were inaugurated in the presence of Group Captain and Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla.
STIF is a fully in-house facility for testing reusable rocket stages under flight-like operating conditions. The facility also supports post-flight inspection and requalification of recovered stages. It supports thrust levels from 1 kN to 200 kN, LOX sub-cooling down to 73 K and full-duration burns of up to 150 seconds. The facility will also be used to inspect and requalify recovered stages after flight.
PROOF will enable the in-house manufacturing of pressure vessels — the rocket component that holds gases or liquids at a pressure significantly different from the outside environment. The new facility can produce more than 10 vessels a month, including vessels of up to 3,500 litres and 350 bar.
“The vision of bringing reusability to launch requires us to think beyond a single flight and build the capability to test, recover, inspect and prepare a stage for its next flight. STIF gives us the ability to test complete stages for the duration of their mission and inspect and requalify recovered stages. This is an important capability as we work towards Mission-02,” said Srinath Ravichandran, co-founder and CEO, Agnikul Cosmos.
Grp Capt and astronaut Shukla said, “India’s space programme is entering an exciting phase, with capabilities being built across the country that will enable increasingly ambitious missions. It is encouraging to see Agnikul continue to expand its capabilities in advanced manufacturing and testing.”
Headquartered in Chennai and incubated at IIT Madras, Agnikul Cosmos develops the Agnibaan family of configurable small-lift launch vehicles. In May 2024, it conducted Mission 01, Agnibaan SOrTeD, from its privately built launchpad at Sriharikota.
Agnikul already designs and manufactures its single-piece, 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engines in-house and develops its avionics and other propulsion and vehicle systems.

india-89c66c632a.headline: India steps up deep-sea mining push to secure critical minerals and strengthen Blue Economy
india-89c66c632a.fulltext:
India is stepping up efforts to develop deep-sea mining capabilities as part of its strategy to secure critical mineral supplies and strengthen its position in the emerging Blue Economy.
The Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) and the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), in association with knowledge partner EY and NITI Aayog, organised a high-level industry outreach workshop on “Deep Sea Mining – Business Opportunities and Strategic Importance” at the Dr Ambedkar International Centre in New Delhi.
The workshop brought together policymakers, regulators, technology developers, research institutions and financial leaders from India and abroad to explore opportunities for greater private-sector participation in deep-sea mining and the development of an integrated maritime industrial ecosystem.
Focus on critical mineral security
Deep-sea mining is gaining strategic importance as critical minerals such as nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese are essential for clean-energy technologies, advanced manufacturing, high-computing systems and electric mobility.
The government sees alternative sources of these minerals as important for strengthening India’s long-term economic and geopolitical security amid growing global demand and supply-chain uncertainties.
India has an exploration contract with the International Seabed Authority (ISA) covering 75,000 sq km in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB). The area is estimated to contain around 366-380 million tonnes of polymetallic nodules.
India is also the first country to hold two exploration contracts for polymetallic sulphides, including a recent agreement covering the Carlsberg Ridge.
Indigenous technology for operations at 5,000 metres
Under the ₹4,077-crore Deep Ocean Mission, India has been developing indigenous technologies for exploring and exploiting deep-sea resources.
NIOT has successfully demonstrated indigenous deep-sea mining crawler systems at depths exceeding 5,000 metres in the Indian Ocean. The achievement is seen as an important milestone in developing subsea engineering capabilities required for deep-sea operations.
The government is now looking at ways to translate these technological capabilities into a wider industrial ecosystem.
From exploration to mine-to-metal ecosystem
The workshop explored the potential for developing an integrated “mine-to-metal” value chain, with opportunities spanning offshore engineering, marine robotics, shipbuilding, metallurgy and downstream industries such as battery manufacturing.
The industry outreach initiative is intended to connect India’s scientific and technological capabilities with private-sector investment and commercial expertise.
It is expected to contribute to the development of future policy frameworks, bankable project roadmaps and an upcoming White Paper on Deep Sea Mining, which will provide a roadmap for greater industrial participation in the sector.
However, commercial mining of polymetallic nodules in international waters cannot begin until the Exploitation Code is finalised by the International Seabed Authority.
The government said the initiative is aimed at preparing India for the next phase of deep-sea resource development while strengthening critical mineral security, indigenous technology and the country’s broader Blue Economy ambitions.

world-b9c8317d4e.headline: Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe
world-b9c8317d4e.fulltext:
The US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby, told European countries they “must not slacken” in their remilitarisation and their backing for Ukraine in a virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv.
The influential Pentagon official praised Ukraine’s recent “stout defence”, which he said proved that Europe was capable of leading the defence of its own continent from Russian aggression rather than relying on the US.
“Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby said at the start of a 50-country virtual meeting of the Ukraine contact group, reflecting what appears to be a warmer tone from the US on Ukraine.
It helped, he continued, “to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken.”
Led by its president, Donald Trump, the US has been pushing for Europe to dramatically increase defence spending and pay to supply American weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, to Kyiv, via a scheme set up by Nato.
The UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include urgently needed Patriot missiles, before the meeting had started.
Boris Pistorius, the German defence minister, pledged in his opening remarks that Berlin would donate a number of older Patriot Pac-2 interceptors from army stocks, and urged other allies of Ukraine to follow suit.
Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks because of a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that have killed civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehouses over the summer.
Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said that Ukraine had been “pretty clear” about what it needed: “Three hundred Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability, $2bn for drones,” and continued contributions to other schemes.
The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, given the cost of each interceptor is estimated at about $3m.
Yevhen Khmara, Ukraine’s newly appointed defence minister, acknowledged that Ukraine’s “situation with ballistics is much more difficult” and which was “precisely down to a lack of Patriot missiles”. It was a situation, he added, that the Kremlin was aware of, and trying to exploit.
The Ukrainian minister also said that Ukraine faced a defence budget gap of €23bn this year, and he hoped that countries would bring forward more funding so that its drone investment programme could continue uninterrupted. Kyiv hopes that the EU will bring forward some of a €90bn two-year loan to help plug the shortfall.
An escalation of the long-range war has meant that the harm to civilians is increasing as Ukraine targets Russian oil refineries and warehouses, while Russian bombing has meant that civilian casualties in Ukraine are at their highest level since May 2022 amid near constant attacks on the country’s cities.
On Sunday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time, to discuss peace proposals, though no breakthrough was made. A day earlier they had visited the Kremlin, which is still pressing for Ukraine to give up territory and make a string of concessions for ending the war.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Trump about the war on Monday, with the two agreeing on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life”.

world-d6d4aa7a20.headline: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
world-d6d4aa7a20.fulltext:
Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
- Published
Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse
Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.
The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.
Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.
When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."
The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.
About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.
After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.
The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.
When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.
The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.
But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.
Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material
"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.
The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.
According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.
TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.
According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.
In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.
"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.
TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.
For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."
For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.
When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000".
TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed.
This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down.
Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings.
TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers.
The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM.
Meta has said it prohibits, external promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images.
One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them".
"We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added.
The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].
Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.
Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.
After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".
But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.
These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.
TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

beyond-your-beat-cdc5daa067.headline: Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit
beyond-your-beat-cdc5daa067.fulltext:
Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit
NEW DELHI: India will host the annual Brics summit on Sept 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At Brics, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies - Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, the UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia - along with 10 other partner countries.The theme of India's 2026 chairship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability', drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to Brics. Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level, including the foreign ministers' and national security advisers' engagements.
India for Brics
Despite political fragmentation and economic imbalances, Brics remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world.
It reinforces India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reaffirms an independent foreign policy.Brics also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to Brics is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to shape the agenda of the developing world. India's moderating influence prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus too on expanding financial architecture, as no govt would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it cannot control. As foreign minister S Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency.Brics also provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. Brics' membership deepens India's trade ties with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from over-reliance on any single partner.
Key challenges for India
The first, of course, is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint Brics declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India will likely focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ring-fence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on US currency. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement while maintaining it is against any common Brics currency or China-centred replacement mechanism.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about Brics' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's economic agenda, India avoided endorsing SCO's 2030 economic roadmap, and it must work with Beijing in Brics on shared objectives, though without letting the forum become a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing.Jaishankar said while announcing the summit that Brics must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit, with key deliverables like a unanimous Brics declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.
To conclude, inclusion of African Union was not the only major takeaway from 2023's G20 summit. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, which allowed a G20 declaration. India can derive confidence from that diplomatic triumph as it heads into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.

other-interests-ed975f9c7e.headline: Why growing seaweed isn’t a climate solution
other-interests-ed975f9c7e.fulltext:
Growing seaweed has long been seen as a way to slow climate change. But this approach is mistaken, a new study argues, as the loss of seaweed emits far more carbon than what is being absorbed by attempts to grow it.
Seaweeds absorb an estimated 3.7 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide through photosynthesis every year, drawing it from seawater, which then draws more CO2 from the air above. They mostly grow near the coast, where they are eventually digested or decomposed, emitting carbon. But fragments of fronds, as well as sugars and carbohydrates from the seaweeds that dissolve in seawater, can sink into the deep sea, sequestering a small fraction of the CO2 as “blue carbon” for thousands of years.
Scientists and start-ups have suggested that seaweed growth, especially kelp, could be expanded to take up more CO2, something the UN has said we will need to do on a massive scale to eventually reverse dangerous levels of global warming.
Advertisement
But there are concerns that cultivating huge amounts of seaweed could backfire and diminish growth of phytoplankton, another important carbon sink. And even the kelp forests we currently have, which are estimated to cover around 640,000 square kilometres worldwide – an area slightly larger than France – are dying off as ocean temperatures reach record highs.
Now, Karen Filbee-Dexter at the University of Western Australia and her colleagues have concluded that, with some 60 per cent of kelp forests in decline, these ecosystems could eventually begin emitting more CO2 than they absorb. Researchers, as well as governments and companies trying to offset their emissions, need to focus on preserving rather than growing seaweed, they suggest.
“Instead of asking how much carbon we can remove with seaweeds, we should be asking how much carbon we can stop from being released as these ecosystems are damaged by climate change,” says Filbee-Dexter.
Some studies have investigated the possibility of removing a billion tonnes of carbon per year with seaweed, but there are already signs that this may not be feasible. For instance, the US carbon removal start-up Running Tide, which raised $70 million to cultivate kelp on wooden buoys that would gradually sink into the deep sea, had difficulty growing kelp in the open ocean and shut down last year.
Other projects have tried to bring back lost kelp forests. An experiment in northern Norway restored 70 hectares of kelp by poisoning seaweed-eating sea urchins, which can multiply when overfishing and hunting remove their predators.
While kelp restoration like this is a win for biodiversity, it only draws down about 50,000 tonnes of CO2 per year. Meanwhile, global kelp loss is emitting an estimated 14 million tonnes of CO2 per year.
The study by Filbee-Dexter and her colleagues also notes that preserving kelp ecosystems is at least eight times cheaper per hectare than restoring them, yet only 2 per cent of kelp forests lie in protected areas.
Firms are also cultivating seaweed to make nori for sushi, animal feed and thickeners for products like ice cream and toothpaste. Fragments of seaweed still drift away and sink into the deep sea, and aquaculture companies like Kelp Blue have promised to eventually sequester and offset hundreds of millions of tonnes of CO2.
Seaweed farming now takes up 4000 square kilometres of ocean. But that’s only about a third of the kelp forest cover lost each year. And after factoring in emissions associated with farming operations – like boat fuel and plastic lines – nine out of 11 seaweed farms were found to emit more CO2 than they sequestered in a study published earlier this year.
“Seaweed restoration and farming is unlikely to be a major climate change solution,” Filbee-Dexter says. “But that doesn’t mean it isn’t worthwhile.”
Restoration can improve biodiversity, and farming can make low-carbon alternatives to fossil-fuel products like fertiliser, she notes.
Pamela Walsh at Queen’s University Belfast in the UK, however, says scientists don’t have a solid enough understanding of how much carbon seaweed sequesters to write it off yet. Macroalgae restoration, conservation and farming can all still be climate solutions, even if their impact has often been exaggerated in the past, she argues.
“Blue carbon is part of the puzzle,” she says. “It can make a contribution. The question is how that is determined and validated.”
PLOS Biology DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003949

other-interests-d5bed8e660.headline: Common painkiller use in early pregnancy linked to smaller ovaries and testes
other-interests-d5bed8e660.fulltext:
Girls whose mothers took paracetamol (acetaminophen) during pregnancy had smaller ovaries at three months old, on average, than those whose mothers didn’t take the drug, according to a study of about 300 infant girls in Denmark. Infant boys whose mothers took paracetamol had smaller testes on average too, the study found.
That doesn’t prove paracetamol caused the reduction in the average size of ovaries and testes, though – this association could be a result of the conditions that led to the women taking paracetamol during pregnancy, or even due to chance alone. Nor is it clear whether having smaller ovaries or testes as an infant affects fertility in adulthood. However, the findings are in line with separate studies done in rats and mice, in isolated human ovaries and in human embryonic cells.
“We still recommend that pregnant women should use paracetamol with high fever or strong pain,” says Margit Bistrup Fischer at Copenhagen University Hospital–Rigshospitalet. Not doing so can be risky, she says.
Advertisement
But most of the women in the study used paracetamol for headaches or musculoskeletal pain, rather than fevers, and could have managed their pain or discomfort in other ways, such as via rest, heat treatment or physiotherapy, says Fischer.
“We should have a dialogue about when paracetamol is actually necessary,” she says. “It is still a drug and it does have side effects. Maybe it shouldn’t be the first thing that we grab when we have discomfort.”
The issue is that there are almost no safe drug-based alternatives to paracetamol for pregnant women. Most other painkillers aren’t recommended because they can cause congenital conditions.
Fischer’s team recruited 685 pregnant women during their first trimester, who were asked about their use of medicines every two weeks. They had an fetal ultrasound during their third trimester, and 302 daughters were examined around three months after birth.
Those exposed to paracetamol as a fetus had, on average, 40 per cent smaller ovaries by volume, 13 per cent smaller uteruses by volume and 23 per cent fewer ovarian follicles – the sacs that nurture immature eggs – compared with those who weren’t exposed. Higher doses were associated with a bigger effect, says Fischer, but no women took more than the recommended daily maximum of 4000 milligrams.
The researchers also analysed data from another study on 1210 girls born in Copenhagen between 1997 and 2002, and found a link between fetal exposure to paracetamol and smaller ovaries during adolescence.
In animal studies, such effects led to reduced fertility and earlier reproductive ageing, but it isn’t clear whether this applies to people. “We cannot say anything about the reproductive consequences for these girls,” says Fischer. That will require long-term follow-up, which is hard to do.
The team also examined the boys who were born to the 685 women. “We do see a difference, on average, in the boys as well,” says Fischer. “[They] have a reduced testicular volume.”
Animal studies suggest this could affect fertility in adulthood, but again it is still unclear if this will be the case for the boys. “We can’t say anything about that because our cohort does not follow them that long,” she says.
A paper describing the findings in girls was published today. A separate paper describing the findings in boys has been accepted by the same journal, but not yet published, says Fischer.
“It is still too early to sound the alarm, and to remove this tool from the therapeutic arsenal for treating pain and fever,” says Séverine Mazaud-Guittot at the National Institute of Health and Medical Research in France, who, in 2022, co-authored research showing that paracetamol impairs the development of isolated human ovaries.
But this latest study, along with one from last year showing that paracetamol affects the proliferation of human embryonic cells, suggest that the precautionary principle should be applied, especially during the first trimester, says Mazaud-Guittot.
“Raising awareness of alternative, non-pharmacological methods should help to encourage a reduction in the use of medication for the treatment of various mild pains,” she says.
“This paper would not change my practice or advice,” says Dimitrios Siassakos at University College London. The team carried out a number of different statical analyses, he says, and the more of these you do, the greater the odds of getting a statistically significant association by chance.
“I do agree that we cannot exclude the possibility of chance findings,” says Fischer. “[But] adjusting for multiple testing could mean that we fail to detect a real effect.”
Another issue is that people taking these medications could be sicker, including with one of the many infections that affect fetal development. They might also eat and behave differently, or vary genetically, says Brian Lee at the University of Pennsylvania. The team tried to take account of such confounding factors, but couldn’t completely rule them out.
“I would not jump to the conclusion that the statistical association observed is a causal association,” says Lee. He thinks there should be further studies into this, but establishing a causal link, if there is one, won’t be easy. A trial in which women were randomly assigned to take paracetamol or not would be the best way, but this would be unethical in pregnant women, says Fischer.
There have been claims that taking paracetamol during pregnancy increases the risk of autism, but the evidence suggests otherwise. “This in no way changes the conclusion that paracetamol is not linked to autism, as multiple studies featuring millions of pregnancies across Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan have shown,” says Lee.
Human Reproduction Open DOI: 10.1093/hropen/hoag074

Turing Award and Fields Medal Laureates Join Global AI Leaders to Explore Scientific Discovery and the Future of Intelligence
HONG KONG, Sept. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit will take place in Hong Kong on December 16-17, 2026, bringing together Turing Award and Fields Medal laureates, leading scientists, AI founders and technical builders, technology industry leaders, sovereign funds and long-term investors, policy representatives, and a new generation of young scientists.
The 2026 Summit was initiated by the Heidelberg Laureate Forum (HLF) and is jointly organized by Laureates City and Symbiosis Science, with the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and the International Mathematical Union (IMU) as supporting partners.
A defining feature of this year's program is the convergence in Hong Kong of three major international scientific communities spanning mathematics and computer science. Centered on AI for Science, the program will extend beyond the two-day Summit to include a Turing Award-themed exhibition, the Masters of Abstraction Gala Dinner, and the continuation of Symbiosis Rising Minds, creating a broader platform that connects foundational scientific thinking, frontier AI, public science communication, emerging talent and long-term collaboration.
As artificial intelligence begins to participate in scientific hypothesis generation, experimental design, drug discovery and materials research - while foundation models, chips, data centers and energy systems increasingly form a new layer of technological infrastructure - the boundary between scientific discovery and artificial intelligence is being redrawn.
When AI begins to participate in discovery itself, how should we redefine science and intelligence?
HLF, ACM and IMU: International Scientific Communities Converge in Hong Kong
One of the defining characteristics of Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 is the international scientific network behind it.
Established in 2013 and initiated by the Klaus Tschira Foundation, the Heidelberg Laureate Forum is one of the world's most influential intergenerational platforms in mathematics and computer science. Each year, around 200 outstanding young researchers from across the world meet leading mathematicians and computer scientists in Heidelberg for sustained scientific exchange.
The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), founded in 1947, is one of the world's leading professional organizations for computing and presents the ACM A.M. Turing Award.
The International Mathematical Union (IMU), founded in 1920, is a central international organization for the advancement of mathematics. It supports the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM), held every four years, and oversees the awarding of the Fields Medal.
Together, these institutions connect a scientific network spanning foundational mathematics, computer science and artificial intelligence. Their presence in Hong Kong will further strengthen links between the world's leading scientific communities, Asia's AI ecosystem, technology capital and the next generation of researchers.
From the Turing Award and Fields Medal to AI for Science
Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 goes beyond the format of a traditional academic forum. This year, the conversation expands from mathematics and computer science into AI for Science - one of the fastest-moving frontiers in global technology.
Over the past several years, AI has moved from being primarily an assistive tool toward becoming part of the core scientific workflow. From protein-structure prediction and drug discovery to advanced materials, energy systems, manufacturing and scientific computing, AI is increasingly involved in complex research processes that were once driven almost entirely by human experts.
At the same time, AI itself is becoming infrastructure, creating an increasingly visible chain of interdependence:
Science → Models → Compute → Energy → Industry → Capital
Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 will explore this transformation through six core themes: the foundational science of intelligence; AI-enabled scientific discovery; frontier foundation models and agents; sovereign compute and energy; the future economy and strategic capital; and decarbonization and green intelligence.
AI × Compute × Energy: The Next Infrastructure Frontier
As foundation models continue to scale, demand for chips, data centers and power systems is rising rapidly. Compute is no longer only a technical consideration; it is becoming strategic infrastructure with implications for national AI competitiveness, energy security and industrial development.
AI is also reshaping the energy system in return. Machine learning is increasingly being applied to smart grids, energy dispatch, storage, advanced materials, carbon management and industrial decarbonization, giving rise to another emerging chain:
AI → Compute → Energy → Carbon → Green Industry → Capital
The Summit will therefore ask not only what comes next for large models, but a more enduring question: who will build the next generation of infrastructure for the AI era?
Scientists, AI Builders and Long-Term Capital at the Same Table
Another defining feature of Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 is its ambition to narrow the distance between science, industry and capital.
The Summit is expected to convene not only Turing Award and Fields Medal laureates, but also founders and technical leaders building the next generation of foundation models, AI agents, robotics and AI infrastructure, alongside sovereign investors, global asset managers, family offices, venture capital, private equity and long-term technology capital.
- Those defining the next scientific questions;
- Those building the next generation of intelligent systems;
- Those allocating capital for the decade ahead.
Turing Award-Themed Exhibition: Bringing the Ideas That Shaped Computing to the Public
Alongside the two-day Summit, Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 also plans to present a Turing Award-themed exhibition in Hong Kong.
The exhibition will trace the development of computer science through archival images of scientists, personal stories, landmark scientific achievements and historical materials, highlighting the people and ideas that helped shape modern computing and artificial intelligence.
If the Summit is focused on the future of AI, the exhibition asks audiences to look backward as well: what scientific ideas, breakthroughs and generations of researchers made today's AI possible?
The exhibition will extend the event beyond the conference room, using science-centered storytelling to connect research, the city and the wider public.
From the scientific contributions of Turing Award laureates to the evolution of computer science into today's AI era, the exhibition will become an important part of Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit's effort to connect scientific history, future intelligence and public engagement.
Gala Dinner: A High-Level Forum for Science, AI and Global Capital
During the Summit, the Masters of Abstraction Gala Dinner will be held at Conrad Hong Kong, creating a more intimate setting for senior figures from science, AI and global capital to connect in depth.
In contrast to the daytime Summit program, the Gala Dinner will bring together leading scientists, AI company executives, sovereign capital, family offices, industry leaders and representatives of major institutions in a private, high-level environment.
The evening will center on AI × Science × Sovereign Capital, with a welcome reception, special conversations and dinner designed to create deeper connections across science, technology, industry and capital.
The daytime program explores the future; the evening is designed to connect the people who may help build it together.
From Today's Leading Scientists to the Next Generation of Rising Minds
Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 will also look beyond the scientists who have already changed the world, toward the next generation whose work may shape what comes next.
Following its launch in Singapore, the Symbiosis Rising Minds program will continue and expand in Hong Kong.
The program is designed for young scientific talent worldwide. It aims to invite leading scientists and professors to frame important questions for the future, identify young people with original ways of thinking and long-term research potential, and support their continued exploration through international scientific networks, intergenerational exchange and sustained research support.
Unlike a conventional competition, Rising Minds is less interested in who can produce the fastest standard answer than in deeper questions:
- Who can formulate a genuinely new question?
- Who sees possibilities outside established paths?
- Who may become part of the next generation to change science?
Hong Kong: Connecting Global Science, China's Technology Ecosystem and International Capital
Hong Kong was selected not only as a venue, but as a strategic point of connection. The city links global universities, scientific communities, international institutions and capital markets on one side, while maintaining close ties with mainland China's AI companies, advanced manufacturing, technology industries and the wider Greater Bay Area innovation ecosystem on the other.
As global AI competition expands from model performance into a system-level contest involving science, compute, energy, industry and capital, Hong Kong is well positioned to serve as a bridge between global scientific and technology resources and China's innovation ecosystem.
From the convergence of HLF, ACM and IMU, to the Turing Award-themed exhibition, AI for Science Summit, Gala Dinner and Rising Minds, Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit aims to use Hong Kong as a long-term gateway for global dialogue across science and artificial intelligence.
Beyond a Summit: Building a Long-Term Scientific Network
Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit 2026 will connect science, artificial intelligence, industry, the public and long-term capital through keynote speeches, panels, fireside conversations, closed-door exchanges, a thematic exhibition and a high-level Gala Dinner.
Its longer-term ambition, however, extends beyond a single event. Centered on AI for Science, Masters of Abstraction & AI4SCI Summit aims to develop an international collaboration network linking leading scientists, AI companies, emerging researchers, industrial resources and long-term capital.
From world-class scientific communities to the next generation of AI builders; from mathematics and computer science to life sciences, materials, energy and industry; from scientific discovery and public science communication to compute infrastructure and long-term capital - a new technological era is taking shape where these forces converge.
"The future will not be built by science, artificial intelligence or capital alone. It will be built where they converge."
